script.opening: "Doctor, I keep getting these horrendous jolts of pain in the right side of my face — like an electric shock or a stabbing — they last only seconds but they’re unbearable. They go off when I brush my teeth, chew, wash my face, or even a breeze hits me. I’m scared to eat or talk now. In between I’m fine. What is this?"

facts.text: Right side only: across the cheek and down into the jaw (points to it on camera). Started about 2 months ago, getting more frequent — "dozens a day now". Each jolt lasts a second or two, sometimes a burst of several. Completely pain-free in between.
Brushing teeth, chewing, talking, washing or putting on make-up, a cold wind. Has stopped brushing the right side. Covers her face with a scarf outdoors.

No numbness or tingling in the face. No weakness, no double vision, no hearing loss, no problems with eyesight or balance. No pain on both sides. No headache, no scalp tenderness, no jaw pain on chewing that builds up. Never had episodes of numbness or blurred vision in the past. No rash.
Saw her dentist 3 weeks ago "thinking it was a tooth"; the dentist found nothing and said it didn’t look dental. "It doesn’t feel like toothache."
Living on soup and yoghurt through a straw; clothes looser — thinks she has lost about half a stone. Drinking enough.

Generally well. Takes no regular medicines; tried paracetamol and ibuprofen — no help. No allergies. Postmenopausal (periods stopped at 52). Of Han Chinese descent on her mother’s side (only if asked about ethnicity/family origin).

Exhausted, dreads every meal, stopped going to her choir. "Tired and fed up" but no thoughts of harming herself. Lives with husband, Peter. Works as a receptionist at a hotel — talking all day is now agony. Drives.

Speak carefully, holding still; flinch and stop mid-sentence once when a jolt comes. You are frightened something serious is causing it. Relief if the doctor names the condition and explains it is treatable. Ask about side effects if a medicine is offered.

ice.ideas: "At first I thought it was a tooth. Now I don’t know."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — fear of a brain tumour ("a growth, maybe") because her sister-in-law had a tumour that started with face pain. Also dreads it never ending.
ice.expectations: "Something that stops the pain, and to know it’s not something terrible."

cues: "I’m scared to eat or talk now" — impact on eating, work and mood.
"The dentist couldn’t find anything" — she has already been bounced once.
"A growth, maybe" (if worries are explored) — the fear to address after the red-flag screen.

checkpoints.text: Recognises TRIGEMINAL NEURALGIA — paroxysmal, severe, unilateral, electric-shock/stabbing facial pain in a trigeminal division lasting seconds, triggered by innocuous stimuli to trigger zones, with pain-free/refractory intervals
Distinguishes it from dental pain (considers/excludes a dental cause), cluster headache, migraine, TMJ pain and giant cell arteritis

EXPLICITLY screens RED FLAGS for a SECONDARY cause (younger age at onset, often quoted as under 40, bilateral symptoms, facial sensory loss, other cranial-nerve/neurological signs, MS features) warranting neurology referral and MRI

Treats first-line with CARBAMAZEPINE (NICE CG173; BNF start 100 mg once or twice daily, titrated) with baseline FBC, U&E and LFTs (HLA-B*1502 first if of Han Chinese or Thai origin) and counsels side-effects/monitoring — hyponatraemia, blood dyscrasia, LFTs, rash (incl. rare SJS), interactions (enzyme inducer), contraception only if still needed (CoSRH) — with specialist advice if intolerant/refractory

Acknowledges and addresses the QUALITY-OF-LIFE impact (eating/talking/washing fear, weight loss, low mood — asking directly about suicidal thoughts, NICE NG225) and refers to NEUROLOGY (confirmation, red flags, refractory pain, surgical options)
Responds to her fear and exhaustion with empathy, conveys that the condition is recognised and treatable, and checks understanding of the medication plan
Explains the diagnosis and reasoning clearly (why it is not dental pain/migraine) and the carbamazepine counselling without overwhelming her

Safety-nets and follows up: rash/unwell on carbamazepine → stop and seek help, monitoring bloods (sodium/FBC/LFTs), review of response and titration, urgent review for red-flag/secondary features, and neurology referral — pattern recognition + first-line treatment + secondary-cause screen

worked.txt: "What you’re describing — sudden electric-shock jolts in the face, set off by touch, chewing or a breeze, lasting seconds with normal periods in between — is a recognised condition called trigeminal neuralgia, a nerve pain in the face. It’s not your teeth, even though it can feel like it, and it’s treatable."

"Let me check a few things to be thorough — is it ever both sides? Any numbness in your face, double vision, weakness, or other neurological symptoms? … No. I’d like to see you in person today to check the feeling in your face, the blink reflex and the other nerves — if those are normal too, that’s reassuring it’s the common, primary type."

"The first-line treatment is a tablet called carbamazepine, which calms the nerve. We start low — 100 milligrams once or twice a day — and build up slowly to the lowest dose that works. It works well for most people, so there’s real hope of getting on top of this."

"A few important things with it: it can cause dizziness, lower your blood sodium, and rarely affect the blood count or liver, so I’ll do blood tests before you start and again soon after. If you get any rash, fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers or unusual bruising, or feel unwell, stop it and contact us urgently. It also interacts with many other medicines, so always mention it when something new is prescribed."

"This is exhausting and frightening — being scared to eat or talk is a big deal, and it can really get you down. We’ll treat the pain, and tell me how you’re coping in yourself too. Has it ever made you feel you can’t go on?"

"I’ll refer you to neurology to confirm things and discuss options if the tablets don’t fully control it — including procedures that can help. Come back if it’s not improving, if you get a rash or feel unwell on the tablet, or if any numbness or new symptoms appear."

f.learning: PAROXYSMS of sudden, severe, UNILATERAL, STABBING/ELECTRIC-SHOCK facial pain lasting seconds in a trigeminal-nerve division (commonly maxillary/mandibular), TRIGGERED by innocuous stimuli to "trigger zones" (light touch, chewing, tooth-brushing, washing the face, cold breeze, talking) with pain-free/refractory intervals, is the classic picture of TRIGEMINAL NEURALGIA. Distinguish it from dental pain (usually continuous/throbbing, not touch-triggered paroxysms — patients often see a dentist first), cluster headache (longer, orbital, autonomic), migraine, TMJ pain, sinusitis and giant cell arteritis. Critically, screen the RED FLAGS suggesting a SECONDARY cause (an underlying lesion such as multiple sclerosis or a compressive vascular/tumour lesion): younger age at onset (often quoted as under 40), BILATERAL symptoms, facial SENSORY LOSS/numbness, other cranial-nerve or neurological signs, deafness, MS/optic features, or atypical continuous pain — which warrant neurology referral and MRI (the cranial nerve examination is done face to face); classic unilateral TN in an older patient with a normal neuro exam is usually primary, but the screen must be explicit. Treat first-line with CARBAMAZEPINE (NICE CG173, 2013; BNF: start 100 mg once or twice daily, increase gradually to the lowest effective dose), with baseline FBC, U&E (sodium) and LFTs and HLA-B*1502 testing first in people of Han Chinese or Thai origin, counselling side-effects and monitoring — dizziness/ataxia, HYPONATRAEMIA, blood dyscrasias, LFT derangement, rash (including rare serious SJS/TEN — stop and seek help), many drug interactions (enzyme inducer), and contraception only if still needed (CoSRH) — with alternatives (oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine, gabapentin, baclofen) if intolerant/refractory, guided by specialist advice as NICE CG173 advises. Acknowledge the major quality-of-life impact (fear of eating/talking/washing, weight loss, low mood — ask directly about suicidal thoughts, NICE NG225) and refer to neurology for confirmation, red flags (with MRI), refractory pain, or surgical options (e.g. microvascular decompression). The hidden agenda is fear and exhaustion (and possible dental bouncing); the skill is confident pattern recognition, first-line carbamazepine with proper counselling, the explicit red-flag screen, and referral.

knowledge.summary: Seconds-long, electric-shock pains in the right cheek and jaw, set off by brushing, chewing, washing or a breeze, with normal periods in between, is trigeminal neuralgia. The GP must name it confidently, screen explicitly for features of a secondary cause, examine the cranial nerves, start carbamazepine (NICE CG173) with proper counselling and baseline bloods, and take the impact on eating and mood seriously.

points.t: Brief paroxysms of severe stabbing or electric-shock pain in one or more branches of the trigeminal nerve, usually the cheek or jaw, on one side. Triggered by light touch, chewing, talking, brushing teeth, washing or cold air. Pain-free between attacks, often with a short refractory period after an attack.

No clinical feature reliably excludes a secondary cause, so MRI is part of the early work-up for everyone. Features that suggest multiple sclerosis or a compressive lesion make MRI and neurology referral urgent: sensory loss in the face, other cranial nerve signs, hearing loss, bilateral pain, onset at a young age (often quoted as under 40), a history of optic neuritis or other neurological symptoms, or continuous background pain. Examine facial sensation, corneal reflex and the other cranial nerves.

Dental causes (usually continuous, throbbing, provoked by hot or cold on a tooth), temporomandibular disorder, sinusitis, cluster headache (orbital pain lasting minutes to hours with autonomic features), post-herpetic neuralgia, and giant cell arteritis in anyone over 50 with new head or jaw pain (ask about jaw claudication, scalp tenderness and visual symptoms).

NICE CG173 [1]: offer carbamazepine as initial treatment for trigeminal neuralgia. It is the exception to the usual neuropathic pain drugs (amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin, pregabalin). BNF: start 100 mg once or twice daily and increase gradually to the lowest effective dose; the dose can often be reduced during remission. If carbamazepine fails, is not tolerated or is contraindicated, NICE CG173 advises seeking specialist advice and considering early referral.

BNF: warn about blood, liver and skin disorders. Stop and seek help at once for rash, fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers, bruising or bleeding. Check FBC, U&E (sodium) and LFTs at baseline and periodically: hyponatraemia is a known effect. BNF: HLA-B*1502 testing before starting in people of Han Chinese or Thai origin. Dizziness and unsteadiness are common early. It is a strong enzyme inducer: check every co-prescribed drug, and where contraception is still needed, CoSRH [2] recommends a copper IUD, LNG-IUS or DMPA.

Pain on eating causes weight loss and dehydration; severe trigeminal neuralgia carries a real risk of low mood and suicidal thoughts, so ask directly (NICE NG225 [3]: no risk scores, a shared safety plan). Refer to neurology for red flags, diagnostic doubt or poor response; neurosurgical options such as microvascular decompression exist for refractory pain.

model.text: Hello Mrs Boll, I’m Dr Ahmed. What’s been happening?

Doctor, I keep getting these horrendous jolts of pain in the right side of my face, like an electric shock or a stabbing. They last only seconds but they’re unbearable. They go off when I brush my teeth, chew, wash my face, or even when a breeze hits me. I’m scared to eat or talk now. In between I’m fine. What is this?
That sounds really frightening, and exhausting. I’d like to ask a few questions so I can give you a proper answer.
model.why: Acknowledges distress and agrees the agenda

model.text: Can you show me exactly where the pain goes?
(points) Here, across my cheek and down into my jaw. Always this side.
Has it ever affected the other side, or your forehead or eye?
No, only here.
Between the attacks, is there any ache or constant pain, or is it completely gone?
model.why: Continuous pain would suggest a secondary cause

model.text: Completely gone. That’s the strange thing.
Have you noticed any numbness in your face, double vision, trouble hearing, weakness, or problems with your balance? Or ever had a spell of blurred vision in one eye?
No, nothing like that.
Any pain in your jaw muscles when chewing that builds up, tenderness on your scalp, or changes in your vision? And have you seen a dentist about it?
No scalp or eye problems. I did wonder if it was a tooth, but it doesn’t feel like toothache.
How are you managing with eating and drinking? Have you lost weight?
I’m eating soft things, very little. My clothes are looser.
Do you take any regular medicines, including anything from the chemist? And any allergies?
model.why: Medication and allergy check before carbamazepine

model.text: Nothing regular. No allergies I know of.
Pain like this wears people down. How has your mood been? Has it ever made you feel you can’t go on?
I’m tired and fed up. I dread every meal. But no, I wouldn’t do anything.
Thank you for telling me. What have you been worried this might be?
Something serious. A growth, maybe.

Let me examine the nerves in your face and head. (Examines facial sensation in all three divisions, corneal reflex, jaw and facial muscles, eye movements, hearing and the other cranial nerves.) Everything is normal.

This is trigeminal neuralgia. The trigeminal nerve carries feeling from your face, and it sends out sudden bursts of pain when something light touches a trigger area. The pattern you describe is typical, your nerves examine normally and it’s on one side only, so this looks like the common type rather than something growing. I’ll still ask the neurologists to see you, and arrange an MRI scan, which is routine for this, to make sure nothing is pressing on the nerve.
model.why: Names diagnosis; addresses fear of a tumour honestly

model.text: So it’s not my teeth?
It doesn’t sound like it. Tooth pain tends to be constant and throbbing, not these sudden shocks.

The first treatment is a tablet called carbamazepine. It calms the nerve rather than being a painkiller. We start with a low dose and increase slowly until the attacks settle, then use the lowest dose that works.
Are there side effects?

Dizziness and unsteadiness are common at first, so take care until you know how it affects you. It can lower your salt level and, rarely, affect the blood count, liver or skin. So I’ll do a blood test before you start and again soon after. If you get any rash, fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers or unusual bruising, stop it and contact us the same day. It also interacts with many medicines, so always mention it when you’re prescribed something.
model.why: Counsels side effects, monitoring and interactions (BNF)

model.text: Okay. What about eating?
Soft, lukewarm food and a straw for drinks can help, and a scarf on windy days. I’ll weigh you today. Could you tell me back what you’ll do if you get a rash?
model.why: Practical advice and teach-back of the key safety point

model.text: Stop the tablets and ring you straight away.

Exactly. I’ll see you in two weeks to check the bloods and how the dose is working. Please come back sooner if you notice numbness, double vision, weakness or hearing loss, if you can’t eat or drink, or if your mood gets very low. You won’t have to put up with this pain.

social.t: Fear of eating causes weight loss and dehydration. Soft, lukewarm food and small frequent meals help while treatment takes effect.
Talking and cold air are triggers, so people withdraw socially. Ask how she is coping at home and at work.

legal.t: Carbamazepine can cause dizziness and drowsiness, especially early or after a dose increase. Advise her not to drive if affected; it is an offence to drive when impaired by medicines.
Document the counselling on rash, blood disorders and interactions, and the baseline bloods.

professional.t: Explain why it looks primary and what would change that, rather than promising it is nothing serious.
Carbamazepine is a strong enzyme inducer. Flag it on the record so future prescribers check interactions.

community.t: Many people see a dentist first. Share the diagnosis so unnecessary dental treatment is avoided.
Patient support groups for trigeminal neuralgia offer information and peer support.

redFlags: Facial numbness or other cranial nerve signs
Hearing loss, visual symptoms or past optic neuritis
Jaw claudication, scalp tenderness or visual change (GCA over 50)
Weight loss from inability to eat; suicidal thoughts
ice: Idea: a tooth problem, or something serious

playbook.diagnosis: “This is trigeminal neuralgia, a nerve pain in the face. Your nerves examine normally and it’s one-sided, so it looks like the common type.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The nerve that carries feeling from your face becomes irritable and fires off sudden bursts of pain when a trigger spot is touched. Often a small blood vessel is pressing on the nerve.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried about a growth. The pattern and your normal examination point away from that, and the neurologists will confirm.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the fear of eating; practical food tips; ask about mood directly.
sharedPlan: Carbamazepine, start low and titrate to the lowest effective dose (NICE CG173; BNF)
Baseline FBC, U&E and LFTs; repeat soon after starting
MRI as part of the early work-up; neurology referral for confirmation and options if refractory
safetyNet: Rash, fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers or bruising: stop carbamazepine and seek same-day review
New numbness, double vision, weakness or hearing loss: urgent review
Unable to eat or drink, or very low mood: contact the practice the same day

pitfalls.intro: This station tests confident pattern recognition plus two safety tasks: the secondary-cause screen and safe carbamazepine prescribing. Most marks are lost by prescribing without either.

items.fail: Treating it as dental pain or sinusitis.
items.why: Touch-triggered seconds-long shocks with pain-free gaps are typical of trigeminal neuralgia.
items.fix: Name it and explain why it is not a tooth.

items.fail: Prescribing the usual neuropathic pain drugs.
items.why: NICE CG173 recommends carbamazepine as initial treatment for trigeminal neuralgia.

items.fail: No red-flag screen or cranial nerve examination.
items.why: Sensory loss, bilateral pain or other neurology suggest MS or a compressive lesion needing MRI.
items.fix: Ask and examine explicitly, including the corneal reflex.

items.fail: Starting carbamazepine without counselling or bloods.
items.why: Blood, liver and skin reactions and hyponatraemia are recognised (BNF).
items.fix: Baseline FBC, U&E and LFTs; teach the rash and sore-throat rule.

items.fail: Ignoring the weight loss and low mood.
items.why: Severe trigeminal neuralgia affects nutrition and can lead to suicidal thoughts.
items.fix: Ask directly and give practical eating advice.

items.why: The dose needs titrating and the bloods rechecking.
items.fix: Book a review within about 2 weeks and safety-net new neurology.

timeMap.d: Let her describe the shocks and triggers. Acknowledge how frightening it is.
Site, side, triggers, pain between attacks, numbness, other neurology, hearing, vision, GCA features, dental history, weight, medicines.
Ask directly about mood. Name her fear of a growth.
Cranial nerves including corneal reflex. Name trigeminal neuralgia and why it looks primary.
Carbamazepine low and slow; bloods; rash and blood warning taught back; food tips; neurology; review in 2 weeks.

wordPics.fail: Calls it dental pain or sinusitis; prescribes co-codamol or amitriptyline; no red-flag screen or cranial nerve examination; starts carbamazepine without warnings or bloods.
wordPics.pass: Recognises trigeminal neuralgia, screens red flags, examines the cranial nerves, starts carbamazepine with key warnings and refers to neurology.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: names her fear of a tumour and explains honestly why this looks primary; asks about GCA at 58; checks medicines and allergy before prescribing; arranges baseline FBC, sodium and LFTs; asks about mood directly; gives practical eating advice; confirms the rash rule by teach-back.

avoid.dont: “It’s probably your teeth. See your dentist.”
avoid.instead: “Sudden shocks set off by touch, with nothing in between, is a nerve pain called trigeminal neuralgia.”
avoid.why: Mislabelling delays effective treatment and leaves her in pain.

avoid.instead: “The first treatment for this particular nerve pain is carbamazepine.”
avoid.why: NICE CG173 makes carbamazepine first line for trigeminal neuralgia, unlike other neuropathic pain.

avoid.instead: “Your nerves examine normally and it’s one-sided, so it looks like the common type. A routine MRI scan and the neurologists will confirm it.”
avoid.why: Honest, reasoned reassurance is safer than a blanket promise.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Seconds-long, electric-shock pains in the right cheek and jaw, set off by brushing, chewing, washing or a breeze, with normal periods in between, is trigeminal neuralgia. The GP must name it confidently, screen explicitly for features of a secondary cause, examine the cranial nerves, start carbamazepine (NICE CG173) with proper counselling and baseline bloods, and take the impact on eating and mood seriously.

points.t: Brief paroxysms of severe stabbing or electric-shock pain in one or more branches of the trigeminal nerve, usually the cheek or jaw, on one side. Triggered by light touch, chewing, talking, brushing teeth, washing or cold air. Pain-free between attacks, often with a short refractory period after an attack.

No clinical feature reliably excludes a secondary cause, so MRI is part of the early work-up for everyone. Features that suggest multiple sclerosis or a compressive lesion make MRI and neurology referral urgent: sensory loss in the face, other cranial nerve signs, hearing loss, bilateral pain, onset at a young age (often quoted as under 40), a history of optic neuritis or other neurological symptoms, or continuous background pain. Examine facial sensation, corneal reflex and the other cranial nerves.

Dental causes (usually continuous, throbbing, provoked by hot or cold on a tooth), temporomandibular disorder, sinusitis, cluster headache (orbital pain lasting minutes to hours with autonomic features), post-herpetic neuralgia, and giant cell arteritis in anyone over 50 with new head or jaw pain (ask about jaw claudication, scalp tenderness and visual symptoms).

NICE CG173 [1]: offer carbamazepine as initial treatment for trigeminal neuralgia. It is the exception to the usual neuropathic pain drugs (amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin, pregabalin). BNF: start 100 mg once or twice daily and increase gradually to the lowest effective dose; the dose can often be reduced during remission. If carbamazepine fails, is not tolerated or is contraindicated, NICE CG173 advises seeking specialist advice and considering early referral.

BNF: warn about blood, liver and skin disorders. Stop and seek help at once for rash, fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers, bruising or bleeding. Check FBC, U&E (sodium) and LFTs at baseline and periodically: hyponatraemia is a known effect. BNF: HLA-B*1502 testing before starting in people of Han Chinese or Thai origin. Dizziness and unsteadiness are common early. It is a strong enzyme inducer: check every co-prescribed drug, and where contraception is still needed, CoSRH [2] recommends a copper IUD, LNG-IUS or DMPA.

Pain on eating causes weight loss and dehydration; severe trigeminal neuralgia carries a real risk of low mood and suicidal thoughts, so ask directly (NICE NG225 [3]: no risk scores, a shared safety plan). Refer to neurology for red flags, diagnostic doubt or poor response; neurosurgical options such as microvascular decompression exist for refractory pain.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open start; let her describe the attacks fully.
Eating, weight loss, fear of meals, mood and exhaustion explored.
Picked up “scared to eat or talk” and asked about weight and mood.
Idea (tooth problem or something serious), concern (a growth), expectation (an answer and relief).
Full cranial nerve examination including facial sensation and corneal reflex; baseline FBC, U&E and LFTs; weight; MRI as part of the early work-up, urgent if red flags.
Trigeminal neuralgia versus dental pain, temporomandibular disorder, cluster headache, giant cell arteritis and secondary causes.
Explicit screen for bilateral pain, sensory loss, other neurology, hearing loss, optic symptoms, continuous pain and GCA features.
Named trigeminal neuralgia and explained why it looks primary.
Carbamazepine started low and titrated (NICE CG173; BNF) with safety counselling; neurology referral.
Nutrition, mood and interaction review addressed alongside the pain.
Review in 2 weeks with bloods; rash rule taught back; red-flag and mood safety-net.

social.t: Fear of eating causes weight loss and dehydration. Soft, lukewarm food and small frequent meals help while treatment takes effect.
Talking and cold air are triggers, so people withdraw socially. Ask how she is coping at home and at work.

legal.t: Carbamazepine can cause dizziness and drowsiness, especially early or after a dose increase. Advise her not to drive if affected; it is an offence to drive when impaired by medicines.
Document the counselling on rash, blood disorders and interactions, and the baseline bloods.

professional.t: Explain why it looks primary and what would change that, rather than promising it is nothing serious.
Carbamazepine is a strong enzyme inducer. Flag it on the record so future prescribers check interactions.

community.t: Many people see a dentist first. Share the diagnosis so unnecessary dental treatment is avoided.
Patient support groups for trigeminal neuralgia offer information and peer support.

redFlags: Facial numbness or other cranial nerve signs
Hearing loss, visual symptoms or past optic neuritis
Jaw claudication, scalp tenderness or visual change (GCA over 50)
Weight loss from inability to eat; suicidal thoughts
ice: Idea: a tooth problem, or something serious

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is trigeminal neuralgia, a nerve pain in the face. Your nerves examine normally and it’s one-sided, so it looks like the common type.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The nerve that carries feeling from your face becomes irritable and fires off sudden bursts of pain when a trigger spot is touched. Often a small blood vessel is pressing on the nerve.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried about a growth. The pattern and your normal examination point away from that, and the neurologists will confirm.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the fear of eating; practical food tips; ask about mood directly.
sharedPlan: Carbamazepine, start low and titrate to the lowest effective dose (NICE CG173; BNF)
Baseline FBC, U&E and LFTs; repeat soon after starting
MRI as part of the early work-up; neurology referral for confirmation and options if refractory
safetyNet: Rash, fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers or bruising: stop carbamazepine and seek same-day review
New numbness, double vision, weakness or hearing loss: urgent review
Unable to eat or drink, or very low mood: contact the practice the same day

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests confident pattern recognition plus two safety tasks: the secondary-cause screen and safe carbamazepine prescribing. Most marks are lost by prescribing without either.

items.fail: Treating it as dental pain or sinusitis.
items.why: Touch-triggered seconds-long shocks with pain-free gaps are typical of trigeminal neuralgia.
items.fix: Name it and explain why it is not a tooth.

items.fail: Prescribing the usual neuropathic pain drugs.
items.why: NICE CG173 recommends carbamazepine as initial treatment for trigeminal neuralgia.

items.fail: No red-flag screen or cranial nerve examination.
items.why: Sensory loss, bilateral pain or other neurology suggest MS or a compressive lesion needing MRI.
items.fix: Ask and examine explicitly, including the corneal reflex.

items.fail: Starting carbamazepine without counselling or bloods.
items.why: Blood, liver and skin reactions and hyponatraemia are recognised (BNF).
items.fix: Baseline FBC, U&E and LFTs; teach the rash and sore-throat rule.

items.fail: Ignoring the weight loss and low mood.
items.why: Severe trigeminal neuralgia affects nutrition and can lead to suicidal thoughts.
items.fix: Ask directly and give practical eating advice.

items.why: The dose needs titrating and the bloods rechecking.
items.fix: Book a review within about 2 weeks and safety-net new neurology.
